system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Ms. ___ was admitted due to concerns about delirium and inability to care for herself, following an episode where she locked herself in the bathroom, refused medications, and exhibited confusion. Upon evaluation, her mental status improved and was determined to be secondary to dehydration rather than primary psychosis. Her creatinine was elevated at 2.8, consistent with acute kidney injury in the setting of prerenal dehydration, which resolved with IV fluid rehydration. She remained in normal sinus rhythm, with stable heart function and no signs of acute pulmonary disease. Dry gangrene of the toes was noted, but vascular surgery advised outpatient follow-up without urgent intervention. A care plan was established involving her grandson and home health services to support medication management and activities of daily living, respecting her autonomy. She was discharged home with services on a reduced dose of furosemide, with instructions to monitor weight and follow up with her PCP and vascular surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___, one of your surgical team doctors. You’re here today for amputation of some gangrenous toes. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay, a bit nervous. The toes have been dry and black for months, but I didn’t think it would come to this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. This is the right step. The gangrene developed after your ICU stay and pressor use. The tissue won’t heal, so removing it prevents infection and helps you heal overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that makes sense. I’ve been managing at home, but I know this has to be done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The plan is to remove three toes—first and second on the right, and one on the left. The surgery should go smoothly, and we’ll monitor you closely after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to walk after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be able to walk. You’ll need to stay off your feet for a few weeks, wear special shoes, and we’ll have physical therapy help you before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The surgery is done. We removed the three gangrenous toes as planned. No complications. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it’s over. My chest feels a little tight though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. You have a history of asthma and lung cancer, so we’ll monitor your breathing closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show a slightly high white blood cell count, and you had a fever last night. We’re concerned about infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it from the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your wound looks clean. We did a chest X-ray, and there’s a new opacity in your left lung. It could be pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I’ve had pneumonia before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild right now. Your blood cultures were negative, so it’s likely not in your bloodstream. We’re starting you on an antibiotic called levofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my other medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked. It’s safe with your current meds, including your asthma inhalers and heart medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I take a lot of pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve reviewed your list. You’re on prednisone, which can affect healing and blood sugar, but we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried to get a sputum sample yesterday, but it was contaminated. That’s common. We won’t repeat it unless your symptoms worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t cough anything up. My chest still feels heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re treating based on the X-ray. The pulmonary team agrees—levofloxacin for a week should clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is improving. Today’s chest X-ray shows the lungs are clearer. The pneumonia is responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. I feel a bit better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. Physical therapy saw you this morning. You’re steady with the walker and can manage stairs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used walkers before. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’ll need to keep your feet elevated and avoid putting weight on the surgical side for several weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No driving either, I assume?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not until your surgeon clears you. And no lifting more than 20 pounds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chest X-ray shows your lungs are stable. The pneumonia is resolving. We’re very pleased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with hydrocodone for breakthrough pain. Take it as needed, but not more than every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s constipating though. I’m already on docusate and senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re keeping those. Drink plenty of fluids and eat fiber to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged home health services to help with wound checks and dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I live alone, but my grandson helps when he can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: He’ll be a good support. Make sure he knows the signs of infection—fever, redness, or drainage from the wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll tell him. And I have my follow-up with the surgeon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in two weeks. That’s when they’ll check your stitches and remove them if ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full course of levofloxacin, even if you feel better. It’s important to clear the infection completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. No skipping meds this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today. You’re alert, walking well, and your lungs and wound are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no soaking your feet, keep them elevated, take your meds, and call if you have fever or wound issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. And wear the post-op shoes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—please try to quit smoking. It affects your circulation and healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ve tried before. Maybe this time I’ll succeed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your primary care doctor can help with resources. It’s an important step for your vascular health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make an appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your home health nurse will visit tomorrow to check your wound and review care instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to make sure I’m doing it right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You will. You’ve been very engaged in your care, and that makes a big difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been through a lot. I just want to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re on the right path. Keep up with your inhalers, heart meds, and follow-ups. You’ve got this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’ll get prescriptions for the antibiotic and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll pick them up on the way home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And wear your post-op shoes at all times when up. They protect your feet as you heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: Ms. ___ was admitted for bilateral toe amputations due to dry gangrene, a complication from prior ICU stay and pressor use. She underwent uneventful amputation of three toes. Postoperatively, she developed fever and respiratory symptoms; chest imaging revealed a new left lung opacity, leading to a diagnosis of pneumonia. She was treated with levofloxacin, with clinical and radiographic improvement. Physical therapy cleared her for discharge home with home health services. She was discharged on postoperative day five in stable condition, with instructions for wound care, activity restrictions, and completion of antibiotic course. Follow-up was arranged with surgery and primary care.
